headline: India weighs a tax on rice sold abroad, while gold, silver and copper keep sliding.
summary: India may tax rice sold abroad to keep it cheap at home. That could lift rice prices for buyers in Asia and Africa. Metals kept falling. Gold had its worst week since March, as traders bet on a US rate rise. Copper slumped on doubts about AI spending. Oil slipped again, far below October's $125 average, though attacks near Saudi Arabia go on.
lookback: Gold and silver kept falling, as the last read expected while the Fed sounded tough. Gold had its worst week since March. Oil stayed low: Brent slipped again on Monday, even as attacks near Saudi Arabia went on. The dry monsoon in India is now hitting rice, not just wheat, and the government may tax rice sold abroad. Russia's wheat sales abroad slowed sharply, as the last read's IGC cut hinted. The OPEC+ meeting and FAO's November food prices are still ahead. We again couldn't open Malaysia's palm oil board.

items.title: India may tax rice sold abroad to keep it cheap at home
items.text: India is weighing a tax of up to 30% on ordinary (non-Basmati) rice sold abroad, The Hindu BusinessLine reported on Sunday. It could come next month. A full ban is a last resort. Rice in Indian shops costs over 11% more than a year ago. A weak monsoon (the summer rainy season) meant farmers planted about 4% less rice. World rice prices were already 37% higher in October than a year before. A tax would mean less Indian rice for sale abroad. Buyers in Asia and Africa could then pay more.

items.title: Gold has its worst week since March, and copper slumps
items.text: Gold lost about 9% last week, its worst week since March, The Hindu BusinessLine reported. Silver fell to about $41 an ounce, two thirds below its January record. Traders see a 96% chance that the Fed (the US central bank) raises interest rates in December. Higher rates make gold, which pays no interest, less attractive. Copper briefly sank below $12,000 a tonne on Monday. Doubts about spending on AI (artificial intelligence) data centers hit it. That is about a sixth below October's average of about $14,500. Copper goes into wiring and buildings, so its price is a clue to how strong the economy is.

items.title: Russia ships far less wheat, while Argentina's is the cheapest
items.text: Russia shipped about 1.1 million tonnes of grain from its ports in 1-20 November, Interfax reported. That is less than a third of a year earlier. Its wheat shipments were about a quarter of last year's. Egypt, the biggest buyer, got about 228,000 tonnes, down from 624,000. Argentina's wheat is now the cheapest of the big sellers, the Rosario grain exchange said. That helps buyers like Egypt. World wheat prices were still 37% higher in October than a year before.

items.title: Oil slips to about $91 as attacks near Saudi Arabia go on
items.text: Brent crude (the main world oil price) fell to about $91 a barrel on Monday, Interfax reported. October's average was $125. News of attacks on oil sites and tankers in the Middle East kept it from falling further. On Sunday the Houthis (a Yemeni armed group) struck a power plant and a port in Saudi Arabia. Iran said it will use all available means against the US naval blockade. Cheaper oil could ease gas prices in the coming months. But new attacks could push it back up quickly.
